title: Cheating
coreMove: Look for the thin cover that keeps a visible violation below the threshold for coordinated punishment.
sourcePressure: The source shows cheating as norm-breaking that survives under thin cover when accusation, proof, and common knowledge are hard to assemble.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The writer treats cheating as secret villainy instead of public ambiguity protected by enforcement costs.

sourceAnchors.name: broad-daylight violations with thin cover
sourceAnchors.detail: The source says interesting cheating often happens in public under a thin fig leaf.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The cover does not need to convince everyone; it only has to keep the room from moving together.

sourceAnchors.name: common knowledge requirement
sourceAnchors.detail: The source says weak norms often need common knowledge before punishment can proceed.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Suspicion is not enough until everyone knows that everyone else saw it too.

sourceAnchors.name: discreet communication and ready-made excuses
sourceAnchors.detail: The source names discreet communication and excuses as ways violations evade enforcement.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: A side glance and a ready excuse can do more protection than a locked door.

exampleSpecs.audience: an operations manager spotting a favored vendor being smuggled through process
exampleSpecs.stakes: the committee may approve a biased deal because the excuse sounds procedural
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Michael asks the chair to state the emergency exception in writing before the favored vendor's demo can become the unspoken default.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: The unopened bid envelopes sit beside a demo laptop already plugged in.

exampleSpecs.audience: a teaching fellow noticing quiet collusion around peer marks
exampleSpecs.stakes: the norm is weak because nobody wants to accuse classmates directly
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: It took Juliette two grade cycles to see that identical praise appeared after hallway whispers, so she replaces open peer scores with blind evidence notes.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Juliette two grade cycles to recognize the repeated phrase.

exampleSpecs.audience: a mechanic handling riders who reserve premium wheels through side channels
exampleSpecs.stakes: public excuses make selfish access look like harmless logistics
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: "Anders said I could hold them for fit testing," Rachel says, and the mechanic points to the checkout timestamp everyone can see.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "Anders said I could hold them for fit testing," Rachel says with the wheel bag already zipped.

exampleSpecs.audience: a board secretary preventing a donor relationship from becoming invisible influence
exampleSpecs.stakes: the room suspects the conflict but lacks shared proof
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Kiran slides the signed donor lunch receipt under the conflict-policy line and asks whether the board wants it recorded before the vote.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: The receipt curls slightly where coffee dried along one edge.

exampleSpecs.audience: a host watching VIP exceptions hollow out a public policy
exampleSpecs.stakes: a small excuse can let status bypass the rule all night
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: You have Giulia mark every exception reason on the host stand screen, making the fig leaf visible enough that managers can no longer pretend it is rare.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You see the waitlist shrinking for names that never stood outside.

exampleSpecs.audience: a release captain stopping a senior engineer from slipping a feature through as a bug fix
exampleSpecs.stakes: a mislabeled ticket can make rule-breaking look like maintenance
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: What happens when the bug-fix label carries a whole new settings page behind it?
exampleSpecs.firstImage: What happens when a bug-fix label opens into a settings page?

skillTargets: spot thin fig leaves in public violations
explain why suspicion fails without common knowledge
choose enforcement moves that lower accusation cost without overclaiming

tryThisNowSpec: Find one rule-bending excuse you heard recently. Write the exact cover story and what shared evidence would be needed before anyone could act.
